A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a [[Definition:Sigma-Finite Measure|$\sigma$-finite]] [[Definition:Measure Space|measure space]] and $\NN$ the set of [[Definition:Null Set|null sets]].
Then $\Sigma / \NN$ is a [[Definition:Complete Boolean Algebra|complete Boolean algebra]] on which:
:$\map {\bar \mu} {\eqclass A {} } = \map \mu A$
is well-defined and strictly positive on non-zero elements.

B_source.statement:
Let $B$ be a [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebra]] and $I$ an [[Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)|ideal]] of $B$.
Then $B / I$ is a Boolean algebra in which the elements of $I$ become $0$.

substitutions.the Boolean algebra being collapsed: the sigma-algebra of measurable sets under union, intersection, complement
substitutions.the quotient algebra: the measure algebra of the space

derived.the operations descend to the quotient: union and complement are well defined modulo null sets
derived.the measure descends and becomes strictl: a class has measure zero exactly when it is the zero element

validity_conditions: The null sets form a sigma-ideal: they are closed under subsets and countable unions, which is what makes the quotient respect countable operations.
The measure is constant on classes, since two sets differing by a null set have equal measure, so it descends to the quotient.
Strict positivity is gained rather than assumed: a nonzero class has positive measure precisely because the null sets have been collapsed to zero.
proof_plan: $\Sigma$ is a [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebra]] under $\cup$, $\cap$ and complement.

$\NN$ is closed under subsets in $\Sigma$ and countable unions, by [[Definition:Countably Subadditive Function|countable subadditivity]].
Hence $\NN$ is a [[Definition:Sigma-Ideal|$\sigma$-ideal]].

Collapse $\Sigma$ by $\NN$, so $A \sim B \iff A \symdif B \in \NN$.
The operations descend, and $\map \mu A = \map \mu B$ whenever $A \sim B$, so $\bar \mu$ is well-defined.

If $\map {\bar \mu} {\eqclass A {} } = 0$, then $A \in \NN$, so $\eqclass A {} = 0$.
Hence $\bar \mu$ is strictly positive on non-zero elements.
By $\sigma$-finiteness, every family has a countable subfamily with the same supremum, so $\Sigma / \NN$ is [[Definition:Complete Boolean Algebra|complete]].
{{qed}}
